note: Puzzle Gym — hand-vetted bank served client-side by the reels 🧩 tab. Every answer verified. Each puzzle teaches a transferable technique. Grows over time.

techniques.name: Work backwards
techniques.blurb: Start from the goal or end state and reason toward the start. Great when the finish is more defined than the beginning.

techniques.name: Restate & simplify
techniques.blurb: Rewrite the problem in your own words or as an equation. Half of 'hard' puzzles are just badly-worded easy ones.

techniques.name: Reframe the question
techniques.blurb: Challenge a hidden assumption you're making. The trick is usually a word you read too fast ('shoots', 'uses', 'shorter').

techniques.name: Casework / enumerate
techniques.blurb: Split into a few exhaustive cases and check each. Slow but unstoppable when the options are finite.

techniques.name: Start with the most constrained part
techniques.blurb: Attack the clue or piece with the fewest possibilities first — it collapses the rest.

techniques.name: Assume, then find a contradiction
techniques.blurb: Suppose an answer is true; if it forces an impossibility, it's false. The engine behind most logic puzzles.

techniques.name: Parity (odd/even)
techniques.blurb: Track whether a quantity is odd or even. If an action never changes it, the end state is locked.

techniques.name: Find the invariant
techniques.blurb: Look for something that never changes no matter what moves are made — it decides what's possible.

techniques.name: Pigeonhole principle
techniques.blurb: If you put more items than boxes, some box holds two. Deceptively powerful for 'must there exist…' questions.

techniques.name: Try extreme cases
techniques.blurb: Test the smallest, largest, or weirdest version. Extremes expose the pattern or the exception.

techniques.name: Draw a picture
techniques.blurb: Put it on paper — a diagram, a grid, a table. Your eyes solve spatial and counting problems your head can't hold.

techniques.name: Count two ways / pair up
techniques.blurb: Count the same thing from two angles, or pair items cleverly, to get a total without brute force.

techniques.name: Use symmetry
techniques.blurb: If two things play identical roles, whatever's true for one is true for the other — halves your work.

techniques.name: List possibilities, then narrow
techniques.blurb: Write out the candidate answers, then use each constraint to cross options off.

puzzles.prompt: Three boxes are labelled 'Apples', 'Oranges', and 'Apples + Oranges'. Every single label is WRONG. You may pull just one fruit from one box (no peeking inside). How do you correctly relabel all three?
puzzles.hint: One box's wrong label tells you the most. Which label, if wrong, leaves the fewest possibilities for what's inside?
puzzles.technique_note: Start with the most constrained box — the one labelled 'Apples + Oranges'. Because every label is wrong, that box canNOT be mixed, so it holds only ONE fruit type. Pull from it and you instantly know which.
puzzles.solution: Draw from the box labelled 'Apples + Oranges'. Since its label is wrong, it's actually pure — say you pull an apple, so it's the Apples box. Now the box labelled 'Oranges' can't be oranges (wrong) and can't be apples (taken), so it's Apples+Oranges. The last one is Oranges. One draw solves all three.
puzzles.general_move: When every option is constrained, begin with the piece that has the FEWEST possibilities — it forces the rest like dominoes.
puzzles.answer: Pick from the 'Apples + Oranges' box; whatever you draw is that box's true single type, then the other two are forced.

puzzles.prompt: On an island, knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie. You meet A and B. A says: 'We are both knaves.' What are A and B?
puzzles.hint: Test the assumption 'A is a knight' and see if it survives.
puzzles.technique_note: Assume A is a knight (truth-teller). Then his statement 'both knaves' would be true — but that makes A a knave, a contradiction. So the assumption fails: A must be a knave.
puzzles.solution: If A were a knight, 'we are both knaves' would be true, making A a knave — impossible. So A is a knave, and his statement is false. 'Both knaves' being false means they're NOT both knaves; since A is a knave, B must be the exception: a knight.
puzzles.general_move: Assume one answer, chase the consequences; if they collapse into impossibility, you've proven the opposite.
puzzles.answer: A is a knave, B is a knight.

puzzles.prompt: A frog is at the bottom of a 30-foot well. Each day it climbs up 3 feet; each night it slips back 2 feet. How many days until it climbs out?
puzzles.hint: The naive answer (net +1 foot/day → 30 days) is wrong. What's special about the FINAL day?
puzzles.technique_note: On the day the frog reaches the top, it's already out — it doesn't slip back that night. So track its position at MIDDAY, not at day's end.
puzzles.solution: At the start of day k the frog is at (k−1) feet (net +1 per completed day). At midday it climbs 3 more, reaching (k−1)+3 = k+2. It escapes when k+2 ≥ 30, i.e. k ≥ 28. On day 28 it reaches 30 feet and is out before the night slip.
puzzles.general_move: Watch for the boundary/last step that breaks the pattern — 'off-by-one' traps live at the finish line.

puzzles.prompt: Four people must cross a rickety bridge at night with a single torch. The bridge holds at most 2 at a time, and any pair crosses at the slower person's pace. Their crossing times are 1, 2, 5, and 10 minutes. What's the fastest everyone gets across?
puzzles.hint: It's tempting to shuttle everyone with the fastest person (1). But the two slow people (5 and 10) should cross TOGETHER so the 10 is only 'paid' once.
puzzles.technique_note: The key insight: send the two slowest across together, so the 10-minute person's cost overlaps the 5-minute person's. Use the fastest two to ferry the torch back.
puzzles.solution: 1 & 2 cross (2 min). 1 returns (1). 5 & 10 cross together (10). 2 returns (2). 1 & 2 cross (2). Total = 2+1+10+2+2 = 17 minutes.
puzzles.general_move: When a big cost is unavoidable, arrange things so you pay it only ONCE — batch the expensive items together.

puzzles.prompt: You have two ropes. Each takes exactly 60 minutes to burn end-to-end, but they burn UNEVENLY (half the rope might take 5 minutes or 55). With only a lighter, measure exactly 45 minutes.
puzzles.hint: Lighting a rope at BOTH ends makes it burn out in 30 minutes regardless of unevenness. Why?
puzzles.technique_note: Reframe 'uneven burning' — you can't trust any single point, but a rope lit at both ends always finishes in half its total time (30 min), because the two flames together consume all 60 minutes of rope.
puzzles.solution: At time 0: light rope A at BOTH ends and rope B at ONE end. Rope A burns out at 30 min. At that instant, light rope B's other end. Rope B had 30 minutes of burn left; now lit from both ends it finishes in half that — 15 min. 30 + 15 = 45 minutes.
puzzles.general_move: When a measure is unreliable pointwise, use a symmetric trick (both ends) that only depends on the reliable TOTAL.
puzzles.answer: Light A at both ends and B at one end; when A dies (30 min) light B's second end — B dies 15 min later, at 45.

puzzles.prompt: There are three light switches outside a closed room. One controls a single incandescent bulb inside. You may flip the switches however you like, but you can enter the room only ONCE. How do you tell which switch controls the bulb?
puzzles.hint: A bulb carries more information than just on/off. What else changes when it's been on for a while?
puzzles.technique_note: Reframe 'the bulb tells me on or off' into 'the bulb also tells me warm or cold'. Heat gives you a third state, so one visit can distinguish three switches.
puzzles.solution: Turn switch 1 ON for ~10 minutes, then turn it OFF. Turn switch 2 ON and immediately enter. If the bulb is lit → switch 2. If it's off but warm → switch 1. If it's off and cold → switch 3.
puzzles.general_move: Look for a hidden extra 'channel' of information (heat, time, order) the puzzle didn't hand you directly.

puzzles.prompt: Prove that in ANY group of 6 people, there are always either 3 who all know each other, or 3 who are all mutual strangers.
puzzles.hint: Fix one person. They have 5 relationships. By pigeonhole, at least 3 of those are the same kind (all friends or all strangers).
puzzles.technique_note: Pigeonhole forces structure: with 5 links of 2 types, one type appears ≥3 times. Then a short casework on those 3 people finishes it.
puzzles.solution: Take any person P. Of the other 5, P either knows or doesn't know each — 5 links, 2 types, so by pigeonhole at least 3 links are the same, say P knows A, B, C. Now look at A, B, C: if ANY pair among them knows each other, that pair + P are 3 mutual acquaintances. If NO pair knows each other, then A, B, C are 3 mutual strangers. Either way, a trio exists. (Same argument if P didn't-know ≥3 people.)
puzzles.general_move: Pigeonhole turns 'must one exist?' into a guarantee: more items than categories means a category repeats.
puzzles.answer: Yes — always. Fix a person, pigeonhole gives 3 same-type links, then casework on that trio guarantees a monochromatic triangle.

puzzles.prompt: You have 12 identical-looking balls. Exactly one is a different weight — but you don't know if it's heavier or lighter. Using a balance scale just 3 times, find the odd ball AND whether it's heavy or light.
puzzles.hint: Split 4 vs 4 first. Whatever happens, you must not only narrow the ball down but keep TRACK of the heavy/light direction across weighings.
puzzles.technique_note: Each weighing has 3 outcomes (left, right, balance), so 3 weighings give 27 signals — enough for 24 answers (12 balls × 2 directions). The craft is designing weighings whose outcomes never collide.
puzzles.solution:
Weigh {1,2,3,4} vs {5,6,7,8}.

• BALANCED → odd is in {9,10,11,12}. Weigh {9,10,11} vs {1,2,3}(known-good). If balanced → 12 is odd; weigh 12 vs good to get heavy/light. If {9,10,11} heavy → odd is among them and HEAVY; weigh 9 vs 10 (heavier is it; balance → 11). If light, same with 'lighter'.

• LEFT HEAVY → either one of {1,2,3,4} is heavy or one of {5,6,7,8} is light. Weigh {1,2,5} vs {3,4,6}. If balanced → odd is 7 or 8 (untouched, from light side) → light; weigh 7 vs 8, lighter is it. If {1,2,5} heavy → 1/2 heavy or 6 light; weigh 1 vs 2 (heavier is it; balance → 6 light). If {1,2,5} light → 3/4 heavy or 5 light; weigh 3 vs 4 (heavier is it; balance → 5 light).

• RIGHT HEAVY → the mirror image of the previous case.
puzzles.general_move: When each test has 3 outcomes, plan so the outcomes carve the possibilities into equal thirds AND preserve the extra bit (here, heavy vs light) you still need.
puzzles.answer: Yes, 3 weighings suffice — start 4 vs 4, then branch by outcome as above, always tracking the heavy/light direction.

puzzles.prompt: Three people make statements. A says: 'B is a liar.' B says: 'C is a liar.' C says: 'Both A and B are liars.' Each person always lies or always tells the truth. Who is telling the truth?
puzzles.hint: There are only a few combinations. Try assuming B is truthful and follow the chain.
puzzles.technique_note: Enumerate the true/false pattern. C's claim ('A and B both lie') is easy to test because it's about two people at once.
puzzles.solution: Suppose B tells the truth. Then C is a liar, so C's claim 'A and B both lie' is FALSE, which is consistent (B doesn't lie). A says 'B is a liar' — but B tells the truth, so A's statement is false, making A a liar. Check: A liar, B truthful, C liar. C (liar) claims both A,B lie — false because B is truthful ✓. All consistent. No other assignment holds up.
puzzles.general_move: With a handful of actors, just enumerate the truth patterns — brute honesty beats cleverness here.
puzzles.answer: Only B is telling the truth (A and C are liars).

puzzles.prompt: A bat and a ball cost $1.10 together. The bat costs $1.00 MORE than the ball. How much does the ball cost?
puzzles.hint: The gut answer '10 cents' is wrong — check it: a $1.10 bat + 10c ball differ by only $1.00? No, that's $1.00 difference… test it fully.
puzzles.technique_note: Restate as algebra. Let the ball be x. Bat = x + 1.00. Together: x + (x+1.00) = 1.10.
puzzles.solution: Let ball = x. Then bat = x + 1.00, and x + x + 1.00 = 1.10 → 2x = 0.10 → x = 0.05. The ball is 5 cents and the bat is $1.05 (which is indeed $1.00 more). The intuitive '10c' fails because it makes the difference only 90c… actually it makes the bat $1.00 and the gap 90c — wrong.
puzzles.general_move: When a number 'feels obvious', write the equation instead of trusting intuition — the fast answer is the trap.

puzzles.prompt: If 5 machines take 5 minutes to make 5 widgets, how long would 100 machines take to make 100 widgets?
puzzles.hint: How long does ONE machine take to make ONE widget?
puzzles.technique_note: Strip it to the unit rate: 5 machines / 5 widgets / 5 minutes means each machine makes 1 widget in 5 minutes.
puzzles.solution: Each machine makes one widget in 5 minutes. So 100 machines working in parallel make 100 widgets in the same 5 minutes.
puzzles.general_move: Reduce rates to 'per one' — the scaling trap disappears once you find the unit rate.

puzzles.prompt: A patch of lily pads doubles in area every day. On day 48 it covers the entire lake. On which day did it cover exactly HALF the lake?
puzzles.hint: If it doubles each day, then the day before 'full' it was…?
puzzles.technique_note: Work backwards from the end state. Doubling forward means halving backward: the day before full, it was half.
puzzles.solution: Since the area doubles daily, the day before the lake is fully covered it must have been half covered. Full is day 48, so half is day 47.
puzzles.general_move: Exponential growth hides at the end — 'half' is always just one step before 'full'.

puzzles.hint: Pair the first with the last, the second with the second-last… what does each pair sum to?
puzzles.technique_note: Count two ways / pairing: 1+100, 2+99, 3+98 … each pair makes 101, and there are 50 pairs.
puzzles.solution: Pair the numbers from the outside in: 1+100 = 101, 2+99 = 101, …, 50+51 = 101. There are 50 such pairs, so the total is 50 × 101 = 5050. (General formula: n(n+1)/2.)
puzzles.general_move: Reorder or pair terms so a messy sum collapses into 'how many groups × group size'.

puzzles.prompt: At a party, everyone shakes hands with everyone else exactly once. There were 66 handshakes in total. How many people were at the party?
puzzles.hint: n people make n(n−1)/2 handshakes. Solve for n = 66.
puzzles.technique_note: Each of n people shakes n−1 others, but that double-counts each handshake, so total = n(n−1)/2. Set equal to 66.
puzzles.general_move: 'Everyone pairs with everyone' always means n(n−1)/2 — recognise the handshake pattern on sight.

puzzles.prompt: How many times in a 24-hour day do the hour hand and minute hand of a clock exactly overlap?
puzzles.hint: The minute hand laps the hour hand a fixed number of times every 12 hours — not 12.
puzzles.technique_note: In 12 hours the minute hand gains exactly 11 full laps on the hour hand, so they align 11 times per 12 hours (not 12 — they don't overlap separately at 12 and ~1).
puzzles.solution: Relative to the hour hand, the minute hand completes 11 laps every 12 hours, meeting it 11 times in that span. Over 24 hours that's 11 × 2 = 22 overlaps.
puzzles.general_move: For two things moving at different speeds, count MEETINGS via their relative speed, not their separate positions.

puzzles.prompt: Using only the digit 8 (as many times as you like) and addition, make exactly 1000.
puzzles.hint: You'll need some three-digit 888s and some smaller pieces. How many 8s can appear in the units column so it ends in 0?
puzzles.technique_note: List the useful building blocks (8, 88, 888) and narrow: the units must sum to a multiple of 10. Three 8s give 24 → need the rest to end in 6.
puzzles.general_move: When digits are constrained, control the units column first, then the tens — build the number outward from the last digit.

puzzles.prompt: Ignoring leap years (365 possible birthdays), how many people must be in a room to GUARANTEE that at least two share a birthday?
puzzles.hint: This is the guaranteed version, not the 50%-chance one. Think boxes and items.
puzzles.technique_note: Pigeonhole: 365 possible birthdays are the 'boxes'. To force two people into one box, you need one more person than boxes.
puzzles.solution: With 365 people you could (in the worst case) have all different birthdays. Add one more — 366 people — and by the pigeonhole principle at least two must share, since there are only 365 days.
puzzles.general_move: 'Guarantee a collision' = (number of boxes) + 1. Don't confuse it with the 'probability > 50%' version (which is just 23).

puzzles.prompt: The numbers 1, 2, 3, …, 100 are written on a board. You repeatedly erase any two numbers a and b and write their difference |a − b|. After 99 steps one number remains. Can it be 0? What can you say about it?
puzzles.hint: Does replacing a, b with |a−b| change the parity (odd/even) of the total sum?
puzzles.technique_note: Find the invariant: a + b and |a − b| have the SAME parity, so each move preserves the parity of the sum of all numbers. That parity is fixed from the start.
puzzles.solution: The sum 1+2+…+100 = 5050, which is EVEN. Each operation replaces a,b (sum a+b) with |a−b|; since a+b and |a−b| differ by 2b, the total sum's parity never changes — it stays even. The final lone number equals the final sum, so it must be EVEN. Therefore it can be 0 (even), but never an odd number like 1.
puzzles.general_move: Hunt for a quantity that every move leaves unchanged — that invariant decides which end states are even reachable.
puzzles.answer: The final number is always EVEN (the sum's parity, 5050 → even, is invariant); so 0 is possible, an odd result is not.

puzzles.prompt: Can you make exactly $1.00 using exactly 50 US coins (pennies 1c, nickels 5c, dimes 10c, quarters 25c)? If so, give one way.
puzzles.hint: Lots of pennies will be needed to reach 50 coins without overshooting $1.00. Try mostly pennies plus a few bigger coins.
puzzles.technique_note: Set up the two constraints (coin COUNT = 50 and VALUE = 100c) and search a small case: pick a penny count, see what the rest must supply.
puzzles.solution: One clean answer: 40 pennies (40c) + 8 nickels (40c) + 2 dimes (20c) = 100c, and 40 + 8 + 2 = 50 coins. ✓ (Other combos exist too.)
puzzles.general_move: With two simultaneous constraints (how many AND how much), fix one variable and let the others be forced — then check.
puzzles.answer: Yes — e.g. 40 pennies + 8 nickels + 2 dimes = $1.00 in 50 coins.

puzzles.prompt: How many squares (of ALL sizes, 1×1 up to 8×8) are there on a standard 8×8 chessboard?
puzzles.hint: Count each size separately. How many 1×1? How many 2×2? Spot the pattern.
puzzles.technique_note: Draw it and count by size: an k×k square's top-left corner can sit in (9−k) × (9−k) positions. So k×k count = (9−k)².
puzzles.general_move: For 'count all sizes', count one size at a time and sum — and remember squares of squares (1²+…+n²) show up constantly.

puzzles.prompt: A wooden cube is painted red on all sides, then cut into 27 identical small cubes (a 3×3×3 stack). How many of the small cubes have paint on EXACTLY two faces?
puzzles.hint: Where on a cube do exactly two painted faces meet? Corners have three; face-centres have one.
puzzles.technique_note: Classify by position: corner cubes (3 faces), edge cubes (2 faces), face-centre cubes (1 face), the very middle (0). Count the EDGE cubes.
puzzles.solution: Exactly-two-face cubes sit on the EDGES but not the corners. A cube has 12 edges, and on a 3×3×3 each edge has exactly 1 middle cube (the two ends are corners). So 12 × 1 = 12 cubes have exactly two painted faces.
puzzles.general_move: Classify pieces by their geometric role (corner/edge/face/interior) and count each class — the structure does the work.

puzzles.prompt: Take a standard 8×8 chessboard and remove two diagonally OPPOSITE corner squares, leaving 62 squares. Can you tile it completely with 31 dominoes, each covering two side-by-side squares?
puzzles.hint: Colour the board like a real chessboard. What colours are the two removed corners?
puzzles.technique_note: Every domino, however placed, covers exactly one black and one white square — that's the invariant. So any tileable region needs equal blacks and whites.
puzzles.solution: Colour it black/white. Opposite corners are the SAME colour, so removing them leaves 32 of one colour and 30 of the other. But each domino must cover one of each colour, so 31 dominoes would cover 31 black + 31 white. Since the counts are unequal (32 vs 30), tiling is IMPOSSIBLE.
puzzles.general_move: A clever colouring often reveals an invariant (here: each piece covers one of each colour) that instantly proves something can't be done.
puzzles.answer: No — it's impossible; the two removed corners share a colour, leaving 32 vs 30, but every domino needs one of each.

puzzles.prompt: You have a 3-litre jug and a 5-litre jug and a tap. Neither has markings. Measure exactly 4 litres.
puzzles.hint: You can only ever get amounts you can build by filling, emptying, and pouring between the two. Try filling the 5 and using the 3 to remove.
puzzles.technique_note: Work toward the target: 4 = 5 − 1, and you can create a '1' as the space left after topping up the 3-litre jug from a partially filled 5.
puzzles.solution: Fill the 5-litre jug. Pour into the 3-litre until full → 2 litres remain in the 5. Empty the 3-litre; pour the 2 litres into it. Fill the 5-litre again; pour into the 3-litre (which holds 2, so it takes only 1 more) → exactly 4 litres remain in the 5-litre jug.
puzzles.general_move: Chain fill/empty/pour steps toward the target amount — working backwards from '4 = 5 − 1' points the way.
puzzles.answer: Fill 5→pour into 3 (2 left)→empty 3→move the 2 into 3→refill 5→top up the 3 (takes 1)→4 left in the 5-litre jug.

puzzles.prompt: Can you connect all 9 dots of a 3×3 grid using only 4 straight lines, without lifting your pen and without retracing?
puzzles.hint: Who said the lines must stay inside the square the dots form?
puzzles.technique_note: Reframe the invisible boundary — nothing forces your lines to stop at the outer dots. Extending lines BEYOND the grid is the whole trick (this is the literal origin of 'think outside the box').
puzzles.solution: Yes. Start at the top-left dot, draw right through the top row and keep going PAST the grid; come back down through a diagonal, along the bottom, and up the diagonal — the strokes extend outside the 3×3 square. Because the pen travels beyond the dots, four lines can sweep through all nine. (Sketch it: the classic solution has two lines poking out past the grid's edges.)
puzzles.general_move: When stuck, question the boundary you IMAGINED — most 'impossible' spatial puzzles forbid something the rules never actually did.
puzzles.answer: Yes — but only if you let the lines extend beyond the 3×3 grid ('outside the box').

puzzles.prompt: What has to be broken before you can use it?
puzzles.hint: Think of something useless while whole.
puzzles.technique_note: Reframe 'broken' as a required step, not damage.
puzzles.solution: An egg — you must break it to use it.
puzzles.general_move: A word with a bad connotation ('broken') may be a neutral or required action in disguise.

puzzles.prompt: What gets wetter the more it dries?
puzzles.hint: It does the drying.
puzzles.technique_note: Reframe 'dries' — the thing is the drier, not the thing being dried.
puzzles.solution: A towel: as it dries other things, it soaks up water and gets wetter.
puzzles.general_move: Ask 'who is doing the verb TO whom?' — swap the actor and object of the action.

puzzles.prompt: Two fathers and two sons go fishing. Each catches exactly one fish, yet only three fish are caught in total. How is that possible?
puzzles.hint: How few people can still be 'two fathers and two sons'?
puzzles.technique_note: Reframe the count of PEOPLE — one person can be both a father and a son.
puzzles.solution: There are only three people: a grandfather, his son, and his grandson. The middle man is both a father (to the grandson) and a son (to the grandfather). Three people, three fish.
puzzles.general_move: When totals don't add up, check whether one item is being counted in two roles at once.
puzzles.answer: They're a grandfather, father, and son — three people, so three fish.

puzzles.prompt: A woman shoots her husband, then holds him underwater for five minutes, then hangs him. Ten minutes later they sit down and enjoy a lovely dinner together. How?
puzzles.hint: Every violent word here has a harmless second meaning in one particular hobby.
puzzles.technique_note: Reframe each loaded verb: 'shoots', 'underwater', 'hangs' all belong to another domain — photography.
puzzles.solution: She's a photographer. She SHOOTS his photograph, develops the film in a water/chemical bath (holds it underwater), and HANGS the print up to dry. Then they have dinner.
puzzles.general_move: When a story sounds sinister, look for a single context (a job, a game) in which every scary word turns innocent.
puzzles.answer: She photographed him — shot the picture, developed it underwater, hung it up to dry.

puzzles.prompt: Whoever makes it, sells it. Whoever buys it, never uses it. Whoever uses it, never knows they're using it. What is it?
puzzles.hint: Think about who the 'user' is and why they can't know.
puzzles.technique_note: Reframe 'the user' — the one who can't know is someone who has died.
puzzles.solution: A coffin. The maker sells it, the bereaved buy it, and the person it's used for (the deceased) can't know.
puzzles.general_move: If a 'user' logically can't be aware, ask what state would make awareness impossible.

puzzles.prompt: A man lives on the 10th floor. Every morning he takes the lift down to the ground. In the evening he rides the lift to the 7th floor and walks the stairs the rest of the way — EXCEPT on rainy days, when he rides all the way to the 10th. Why?
puzzles.hint: What does he carry on rainy days that he doesn't on dry ones? How might that help him press a button?
puzzles.technique_note: Reframe the exception: 'rainy days' is a clue about an object (an umbrella) that extends his reach. Consider his physical constraints (he's short).
puzzles.solution: The man is very short. He can reach the ground-floor button and the 7th-floor button, but not the 10th — it's too high. On rainy days he has an umbrella, which he uses to press the 10th-floor button.
puzzles.general_move: Zero in on the EXCEPTION ('except when it rains') — the reason for the special case usually reveals the whole puzzle.
puzzles.answer: He's too short to reach the 10th-floor button; on rainy days his umbrella lets him press it.

puzzles.prompt: You're running a race and you overtake the person in 2nd place. What position are you in now?
puzzles.hint: You took THEIR spot, not the leader's.
puzzles.technique_note: Reframe the careless assumption that passing '2nd' makes you 1st.
puzzles.solution: You're now in 2nd place. Overtaking the runner in 2nd means you take over 2nd — the person in 1st is still ahead of you.
puzzles.general_move: Slow down on relative claims ('the person in 2nd') — passing rank N puts you at N, not N−1.

puzzles.prompt: I am an odd number. Remove a single letter from my name and I become even. What number am I?
puzzles.hint: Think about how the WORDS look, not the values.
puzzles.technique_note: Reframe from arithmetic to spelling — the trick is in the letters of the word.
puzzles.solution: SEVEN. Remove the 'S' and it spells EVEN.
puzzles.general_move: 'Number' puzzles are sometimes WORD puzzles — check the spelling, not just the maths.

puzzles.prompt: What English word becomes SHORTER when you add two letters to it?
puzzles.hint: The answer is almost a description of itself.
puzzles.technique_note: Reframe 'shorter' as a literal word, not a change in length.
puzzles.solution: 'Short' — add the two letters 'e' and 'r' and it becomes 'shorter'.
puzzles.general_move: Take the puzzle's own describing word literally — sometimes the answer IS that word.

puzzles.prompt: 'Forward' I am heavy; spelled backward I am 'not'. What three-letter word am I?
puzzles.hint: Reverse the letters of a word meaning heavy… what do you read?
puzzles.technique_note: Reframe as a reversal (a palindrome-style trick): find a heavy-meaning word whose reverse spells 'not'.
puzzles.solution: TON. It means a heavy weight, and reversed it spells NOT.
puzzles.general_move: For 'backwards' clues, literally reverse candidate words and read what appears.

puzzles.prompt: Name a common English word that contains three consecutive DOUBLE letters (i.e., three pairs of repeated letters in a row).
puzzles.hint: Think of an occupation involving books and records.
puzzles.technique_note: List words with doubled letters and narrow to one where three doubles touch. Occupations and compound words are fertile ground.
puzzles.solution: BOOKKEEPER — the letters run b-OO-KK-EE-per, giving three consecutive double letters (oo, kk, ee).
puzzles.general_move: For 'find a word that…' puzzles, brainstorm a themed category (jobs, compounds) and test candidates against the rule.

puzzles.prompt: What common five-letter English word is still pronounced the same even after you remove its last FOUR letters?
puzzles.hint: The remaining single letter is a letter of the alphabet that already sounds like the whole word.
puzzles.technique_note: Reframe: you need a word that sounds like a single letter's NAME. Then find a 5-letter word that starts with that letter and sounds identical.
puzzles.solution: QUEUE. Remove the last four letters (u-e-u-e) and you're left with 'Q', which is pronounced exactly the same as 'queue'.
puzzles.general_move: When a puzzle plays on sound, think of words that are homophones of single letters (are→R, why→Y, queue→Q).

puzzles.prompt: A man looks at a portrait and says: 'Brothers and sisters I have none, but that man's father is my father's son.' Who is in the portrait?
puzzles.hint: Since he has no brothers, who is 'my father's son'?
puzzles.technique_note: Restate the relationship one clause at a time. 'My father's son' — with no brothers — can only be the speaker himself.
puzzles.solution: With no siblings, 'my father's son' must be the speaker himself. So the sentence becomes: 'that man's father is ME.' If the speaker is the portrait-man's father, then the portrait is of his SON.
puzzles.general_move: Untangle family riddles by substituting each phrase step by step ('my father's son' → 'me') until the relation is plain.

puzzles.prompt: How many rectangles (of every size, including squares) can be found on a standard 8×8 chessboard grid?
puzzles.hint: A rectangle is fixed by choosing two of the vertical grid lines and two of the horizontal grid lines. How many lines are there each way?
puzzles.technique_note: Count two ways via choices: an 8×8 board has 9 vertical and 9 horizontal grid lines. Any 2 verticals + any 2 horizontals define exactly one rectangle.
puzzles.solution: Choose 2 of the 9 vertical lines: C(9,2) = 36 ways. Choose 2 of the 9 horizontal lines: C(9,2) = 36 ways. Each pair-of-pairs makes one rectangle, so 36 × 36 = 1296 rectangles.
puzzles.general_move: Recast 'how many shapes' as 'how many independent CHOICES define one' — then multiply the counts.

puzzles.prompt: From a bag of exactly 3 red hats and 2 blue hats, one hat is placed on each of three people standing in a line (the other two hats stay hidden). The BACK person sees the two hats ahead; the MIDDLE sees only the front person's; the FRONT sees none. The back says: 'I can't tell my hat's colour.' The middle then says: 'I can't tell mine either.' At which point the FRONT person announces: 'Then mine must be red.' How did the front person know?
puzzles.hint: There are only 2 blue hats. What would the back person see that would let them instantly know their own colour?
puzzles.technique_note: Use the back person's uncertainty. Since only 2 blue hats exist, if the back saw two blue hats ahead, it would KNOW its own is red. It didn't know — so the two front hats are not both blue.
puzzles.solution: Only 2 blue hats exist. If the back person saw BLUE on both people ahead, both blues would be used and the back would know its own hat is red. The back was unsure, so the middle and front hats are NOT both blue. The middle person, hearing this, now reasons: if the FRONT hat were blue, then for 'not both blue' the middle's own hat would have to be red — the middle would know. But the middle is ALSO unsure, so the front hat cannot be blue. Therefore the front hat is red — and the front person, hearing both 'I can't tell's, deduces exactly that.
puzzles.general_move: Each 'I don't know' is hard information: it eliminates every scenario in which that person COULD have known. Chain those eliminations.
puzzles.answer: Red. Both 'I can't tell' statements rule out the blue possibilities, forcing the front hat to be red.

puzzles.prompt: Think of any number. Double it. Add 10. Halve the result. Subtract the number you first thought of. What's left — and why is it always the same?
puzzles.hint: Do it with a symbol x instead of a specific number.
puzzles.technique_note: Restate with algebra: let the number be x and carry it through each step symbolically.
puzzles.solution: Let the number be x. Double: 2x. Add 10: 2x + 10. Halve: x + 5. Subtract x: 5. The x cancels, so the answer is always 5, no matter what you started with.
puzzles.general_move: To see WHY a number trick always works, replace the mystery number with a symbol and simplify — the variable cancels.
